title: What does `EXPLAIN` (PostgreSQL/MySQL) show (the query plan the optimizer CHOSE — access method, join order, index usage, estimated rows/cost), how does `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` differ (it RUNS the query and shows ACTUAL rows/time alongside estimates), and why is the first thing you look for a sequential/full-table scan on a large table?
shortTitle: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE — Reading the Query Plan

s1_definition.profdef: `EXPLAIN` asks the database to show the execution plan the optimizer chose for a query without running it — which access method it will use (sequential scan versus index scan), the join order and join algorithms, which indexes it will use, and its estimated row counts and cost. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query and shows the real row counts and real timings alongside the estimates, so you can compare what the optimizer predicted against what truly happened. The first red flag you look for is a sequential (full-table) scan on a large table, because that means the engine is reading every row instead of using an index.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine asking a bank clerk how they will find a transaction. EXPLAIN is the clerk describing their plan: "I'll flip through every page of the ledger" (sequential scan) versus "I'll use the index at the back to jump straight to it" (index scan). EXPLAIN ANALYZE is sending the clerk to actually do it and timing them, then comparing their guess to reality. If a clerk says they'll flip through all ten million pages of the transactions ledger, that is the full-table scan you want to catch and fix with an index.
s1_definition.oneliner: EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose with estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows actuals — and the first thing you hunt for is a sequential scan on a big table.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `EXPLAIN` asks the database to show the execution plan the optimizer chose for a query without running it — which access method it will use (sequential scan versus index scan), the join order and join algorithms, which indexes it will use, and its estimated row counts and cost. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` actually executes the query and shows the real row counts and real timings alongside the estimates, so you can compare what the optimizer predicted against what truly happened. The first red flag you look for is a sequential (full-table) scan on a large table, because that means the engine is reading every row instead of using an index.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine asking a bank clerk how they will find a transaction. EXPLAIN is the clerk describing their plan: "I'll flip through every page of the ledger" (sequential scan) versus "I'll use the index at the back to jump straight to it" (index scan). EXPLAIN ANALYZE is sending the clerk to actually do it and timing them, then comparing their guess to reality. If a clerk says they'll flip through all ten million pages of the transactions ledger, that is the full-table scan you want to catch and fix with an index.

**One line to remember:** EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose with estimates; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows actuals — and the first thing you hunt for is a sequential scan on a big table.

sections.s2_technical:
EXPLAIN prints the plan tree the optimizer selected. Each node is an operation: a Seq Scan reads the whole table, an Index Scan walks an index to find rows, an Index Only Scan answers entirely from the index without touching the table, a Bitmap Heap Scan combines an index with batched heap reads. Join nodes show the algorithm — Nested Loop, Hash Join, or Merge Join — and the order in which tables are joined. Each node carries an estimated startup cost, total cost, estimated row count, and row width. These numbers are the optimizer's predictions based on table statistics.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE goes further: it runs the query and annotates each node with actual time and actual rows, plus how many times the node looped. Now you can compare estimated rows against actual rows. A large gap — say the optimizer expected ten rows but got a million — means the statistics are stale, and running ANALYZE on the table to refresh them often fixes a bad plan. Because EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes, you must be careful running it on statements that write data; in PostgreSQL you wrap it in a transaction and roll back.

The first thing you look for is a Seq Scan on a large table. A sequential scan reads every single row, so on a table with hundreds of millions of rows it is slow. A Seq Scan is sometimes correct — if a query genuinely returns most of the table, scanning is cheaper than an index — but when you expected an index to be used and see a Seq Scan instead, it points to a missing index, a non-sargable predicate (a WHERE clause that wraps the column in a function so the index cannot be used, like WHERE UPPER(name) = 'RAJESH'), or low selectivity where the optimizer decided the index was not worth it.

Other things you read: a Nested Loop with a huge outer table usually wants to be a Hash Join; a Sort node with high cost suggests a missing index that could have provided the order; and the biggest tell of all remains the estimated-versus-actual row mismatch.

The senior nuance is to use the richer formats — EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows shared buffer hits and disk reads so you can see whether the slowness is CPU or I/O, and FORMAT JSON makes the plan machine-readable for tooling.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: a query that finds Rajesh's transactions by his account id is slow in production. We suspect a full-table scan on the huge transactions table.

Problem 1 — we must see the plan, not guess. We model a tiny query planner that reports either a Seq Scan or an Index Scan depending on whether a usable index exists for the predicate, and prints estimated cost.

Problem 2 — estimates can lie. We model EXPLAIN ANALYZE by also running the simulated query and reporting actual rows and time, so we can spot the estimated-versus-actual gap caused by stale statistics.

Problem 3 — a non-sargable predicate defeats the index. We show that wrapping the column in a function forces a Seq Scan even when an index exists, and that removing the function restores the Index Scan.

The code includes a PlanNode model, a MiniPlanner that chooses Seq versus Index Scan, and an ExplainService that prints EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE style output for three queries.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__create_tables.sql (Flyway)
CREATE TABLE transactions (
    txn_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    account_id VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    amount     DECIMAL(15,2) NOT NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);
CREATE INDEX idx_txn_account ON transactions(account_id);   -- lets us index-scan by account

-- Fast (sargable, uses idx_txn_account):
-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001';
-- Slow (non-sargable, function on column → Seq Scan):
-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE UPPER(account_id) = 'SAV2001';
-- Refresh stats if estimates are far off:
-- ANALYZE transactions;
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
planner:
  table-rows: 200000000       # 200M rows — a Seq Scan here is a disaster
  index-depth: 4
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three queries against the 200-million-row transactions table.

Step 1 — Query 1 filters on account_id, an indexed column, with a plain predicate. The planner chooses an Index Scan. EXPLAIN shows the chosen node and a low estimated cost. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it, returns 500 rows in 1.2 milliseconds, and the estimate matches the actual, so no warning fires.

Step 2 — Query 2 wraps the column in UPPER(), making the predicate non-sargable, so the index cannot be used and the planner falls back to a Seq Scan over all 200 million rows. EXPLAIN immediately flags the Seq Scan as a red flag. EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirms it took 4,200 milliseconds.

Step 3 — Query 3 has an Index Scan plan but stale statistics: the optimizer estimated 10 rows while the actual is 5 million. The estimate-versus-actual gap triggers the advice to run ANALYZE to refresh statistics so the optimizer can pick a better plan next time.

Final output:

```
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [INFO] EXPLAIN WHERE account_id='SAV2001': Index Scan (est rows=500 cost=2000.0)
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [INFO] EXPLAIN ANALYZE WHERE account_id='SAV2001': Index Scan est=500 actual=500 time=1.2ms
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [INFO] EXPLAIN WHERE UPPER(account_id)='SAV2001': Seq Scan (est rows=500 cost=2.0E8)
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [WARNING] RED FLAG: Seq Scan on a large table for WHERE UPPER(account_id)='SAV2001'
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [INFO] EXPLAIN ANALYZE WHERE UPPER(account_id)='SAV2001': Seq Scan est=500 actual=500 time=4200.0ms
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [INFO] EXPLAIN ANALYZE WHERE amount>1,00,000: Index Scan est=10 actual=5000000 time=9000.0ms
2026-10-25 17:35:00 [WARNING] Estimate vs actual gap huge for WHERE amount>1,00,000 → run ANALYZE (stale stats)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  SQL query
    │
    ▼
  Optimizer builds plan
    ├─ EXPLAIN          → prints CHOSEN plan + ESTIMATES (does NOT run)
    └─ EXPLAIN ANALYZE  → RUNS query → prints ACTUAL rows + time alongside estimates
          │
          ▼
  Read the plan, first check:
    ├─ Seq Scan on big table?  → missing index / non-sargable / low selectivity
    ├─ Nested Loop huge outer? → prefer Hash Join
    ├─ costly Sort?            → missing index for ORDER BY
    └─ est ≪ actual rows?      → stale stats → ANALYZE table
```


sections.s6_takeaway:
EXPLAIN asks the database to show me the execution plan the optimizer chose for a query without actually running it. It tells me the access method — a sequential scan that reads the whole table versus an index scan that jumps straight to matching rows — the join order and join algorithm, which indexes it will use, and its estimated row counts and cost. EXPLAIN ANALYZE goes one step further: it actually runs the query and annotates each node with the real row counts and real timings next to the estimates, so I can compare prediction against reality. Because it executes, on a writing statement I wrap it in a transaction and roll back.

The very first thing I look for when reading a plan is a sequential scan on a large table, because that means the engine is reading every single row. Sometimes a Seq Scan is correct — if a query genuinely returns most of the table, scanning beats an index — but when I expected an index to be used and I see a Seq Scan instead, it almost always means one of three things: there is no index on that column, the predicate is non-sargable because it wraps the column in a function like UPPER so the index cannot be used, or the column is so low-selectivity that the optimizer decided the index was not worth it. After that I look for a Nested Loop over a huge outer table that should be a Hash Join, a costly Sort that a well-chosen index could have avoided, and above all a big gap between estimated and actual rows, which tells me the statistics are stale and I should run ANALYZE on the table.

In our National Bank of India platform a query filtering transactions by account slowed to seconds in production; EXPLAIN showed a Seq Scan on the two-hundred-million-row table because someone had written WHERE UPPER(account_id) equals a value, which made it non-sargable. We removed the function so the predicate matched the index, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirmed the plan switched to an Index Scan and the time dropped from four seconds to a couple of milliseconds. I also use EXPLAIN with the BUFFERS option to see whether the cost is CPU or disk I/O. The line I remember is that EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with estimates, EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows the actuals, and the first thing I hunt for is a sequential scan on a big table.

---

keyPoints: EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE: see query execution plan
Look for: full table scans, missing indexes, sort operations
Optimize: add indexes, rewrite queries, reduce data scanned
Slow query log: identify queries exceeding threshold
